interviewQuestions.question: Design a product recommendation system for an e-commerce homepage.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd structure this as the same funnel used across recommenders, feed, and search: candidate generation, then ranking, then re-ranking.

For candidate generation at catalog scale, I'd use a two-tower model for the bulk of established items, but merge in a content-based pool (for newer, thin-data items) and a popularity/trending pool (for brand-new users) — no single source covers every cold-start case.

For ranking, I'd score the merged shortlist with user, item, and cross-features, training on a blend of implicit signals (click, add-to-cart, purchase) rather than any one alone, since purchase alone is too sparse and click alone is gameable.

I'd explicitly call out cold start rather than treat it as an afterthought: new users fall back to popularity and onboarding signals, new items lean on content-based candidates and get a small ranking boost to accelerate data collection.

Before full rollout, I'd A/B test against the current system on real revenue/engagement, with guardrail metrics like return-rate and complaint rate running alongside — and critically, keep a holdout group on the old system throughout, since without one a slow regression is undetectable until it's already done damage.

**Testing:** whether you can integrate the full recommender toolkit into one coherent pipeline and treat cold start and safe rollout as first-class parts of the design, not afterthoughts.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: E-commerce recommender design

interviewQuestions.question: Why does a mature recommender system run multiple candidate-generation sources in parallel instead of relying on one good retrieval method?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Each candidate source has a specific blind spot, and no single one covers every scenario a live product actually faces. A two-tower collaborative model, the workhorse for established items, needs enough interaction history to have learned a meaningful embedding for both the user and the item — it structurally cannot produce a good recommendation for an item that was just added five minutes ago, or a user who just signed up, because there's no interaction signal yet for it to have learned from. That's not a tuning problem to fix with a better model; it's a fundamental limitation of what collaborative signal requires to exist at all.

A content-based similarity pool fills exactly that gap for new items — it can recommend based on the item's own features (category, description, image) with zero interaction history required, since it's not depending on collaborative signal at all. A popularity/trending pool fills the analogous gap for new users — with no personalization signal yet available, showing what's broadly popular is a far better default than showing nothing or showing arbitrary noise from an undertrained personalized model.

Running all three and merging results means the system always has a reasonable fallback regardless of which cold-start case it's facing, rather than degrading badly whenever the primary method's assumptions don't hold. This mirrors a broader pattern in production ML: a single sophisticated model that's excellent in its comfort zone but has no graceful fallback for edge cases it wasn't designed for is a fragile system, even if its average-case metrics look great.

**Testing:** whether you can name the specific cold-start gap each candidate source fills, not just list that multiple sources exist as a best practice.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why multiple candidate sources are merged

interviewQuestions.question: You're three weeks into a gradual rollout of a new recommender, and the primary revenue metric looks flat-to-slightly-positive, but you're not sure it's actually safe to ramp to 100%. What would make you confident either way?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A flat-to-slightly-positive primary metric alone isn't sufficient evidence in either direction — it's exactly the ambiguous middle case where the right process matters more than the specific number. My first check is the guardrail metrics running alongside the primary one: return rate, complaint/unsubscribe rate, support ticket volume specific to recommendations. A primary revenue metric that's flat while a guardrail metric is quietly degrading is a real signal the new system might be extracting short-term revenue at the cost of longer-term trust or satisfaction — exactly the kind of regression a single primary metric wouldn't flag on its own, which is the whole reason guardrails exist as a separate, mandatory check rather than an optional nice-to-have.

Second, I'd check the holdout group specifically — a subset of users who never saw the new system throughout the rollout. Comparing the treatment group against that stable holdout tells me what would have happened anyway versus what the new system actually changed; without it, a flat metric could mean "the new system is neutral" or could mean "the whole user base's behavior shifted for external reasons this quarter, masking a real regression or a real improvement equally." A holdout is the only way to separate the system's actual causal effect from background noise or seasonality.

Third, I'd segment the metric rather than trust the aggregate — a flat overall number can hide a meaningful win for one user segment (power users) offset by a real loss for another (new users, or a specific product category), and ramping to 100% on an aggregate-flat number without checking segments risks locking in a regression for whichever segment is actually worse off.

Given three weeks of data with a genuinely ambiguous signal, I'd extend the observation window before ramping further rather than force a decision on insufficient evidence — a false-positive ramp is much more costly to unwind than a delayed one.

**Testing:** whether you know to check guardrails, the holdout comparison, and segment-level effects before trusting an ambiguous aggregate metric, rather than making a binary go/no-go call on one number.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Deciding whether an ambiguous rollout is safe to ramp
